question: An 18-month-old boy presents to the pediatrician by his mother for a routine check-up. The mother has no concerns, although she asks about the "hole in his heart" that the patient had at birth. The patient has no history of cyanosis or heart failure; however, a holosystolic, harsh murmur was noted at the 3- and 6-month check-ups. On examination, the patient is playful and alert. He has met all developmental milestones. The cardiac examination reveals a regular rate and rhythm with persistence of the holosystolic, harsh murmur. What is the most likely cause of the murmur in this child?

options.opc: Defect of the membranous interventricular septum
options.ope: Failure of endocardial cushion to form

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Holosystolic, harsh murmur" -> "Persistence of murmur at 3- and 6-month check-ups" -> "Likely structural heart defect" -> "Defect of the membranous interventricular septum" -> 80% CHAIN: "Holosystolic, harsh murmur" -> "Persistence of murmur at 3- and 6-month check-ups" -> "Likely structural heart defect" -> "Defect of muscular interventricular septum" -> 70% CHAIN: "Holosystolic, harsh murmur" -> "Persistence of murmur at 3- and 6-month check-ups" -> "Likely structural heart defect" -> "Failure of endocardial cushion to form" -> 80%
analysis: The most likely cause of the holosystolic, harsh murmur in this child is a defect of the membranous interventricular septum, also known as a ventricular septal defect (VSD). This is a common congenital heart defect that can present with a murmur and typically does not cause cyanosis or heart failure in infants.
